answer: Treat 'context 56' as two records, not one. The posthole in Trench 3 and the pit fill in Trench 7 are two distinct real-world features (different trenches, different feature types, no evidence they are physically or genetically connected), so they must be two separate CRM entities -- each an instance of CRMarchaeo A8 Stratigraphic Unit (the fill would more specifically be an A2 Stratigraphic Volume Unit). The clash is not an entity-identity problem, it is an identifier-collision problem: two site supervisors each ran their own E15 Identifier Assignment, independently assigning the string '56' (E42 Identifier, via P1 is identified by / P37 assigned) to their own unit. CIDOC CRM's E42 scope note already frames identifiers as unique only 'within the context of one or more organisations', and P1 is identified by is many-to-many (0,n:0,n per its dossier), so nothing in the model requires -- or even suggests -- that two entities sharing an identifier string must be merged. The fix is documentation, not ontology: give the posthole and the pit fill separate entities, each with its own P1/E42 '56', and use E15 Identifier Assignment (P14 carried out by the respective supervisor) to record who assigned the clashing number and when, so the historical mistake is explained rather than baked into the archive as one confused record. I checked whether CRMarchaeo A6 Group Declaration Event applies (it covers separate surviving fragments later recognised as remains of one past whole, e.g. postholes read as one former house) -- it does not fit here, since nothing in the case is an interpretive claim that the two contexts were ever one feature; they are simply unrelated features that got the same clerical number.

rejected_alternatives.why_not: A6 Group Declaration Event is for recognising that two or more separate surviving stratigraphic units (or other E18 Physical Things) are remains of one former whole -- its own examples are things like disconnected stratigraphic units cut by a later ditch, or postholes read as one past wooden house. Nothing in this case makes an interpretive claim that the Trench 3 posthole and Trench 7 pit fill were ever one feature; they are unrelated, so treating '56' as a single merged record via A6 would misrepresent the evidence.

P1 is identified by has quantification many-to-many, and E42's own scope note ties uniqueness to 'the context of one or more organisations', not globally -- so a shared identifier string is not itself evidence of shared identity. A posthole in Trench 3 and a pit fill in Trench 7 fail every identity criterion (location, form, genesis) that would justify one record.
